errors.english: Wrapping themselves around women is like embracing a blazing, spark-strewn fire born of iron.
errors.why: The Tibetan describes the hell punishment itself: they embrace women made of iron, blazing with fire and covered in sparks; it is not a simile for embracing women in this life.

note: A difficult kāvya passage rendered with the general sense intact, but several verse lines are loose or obscure and the hell-torment image is turned into a simile.
Faithful rendering of the general and specific (indirect/direct) characteristics of the truths and the two kinds of wish for liberation.

errors.english: When the words reached their conclusion
errors.why: The Tibetan (Skt. sādhuvāde) says when the gods' cry of praise spread to the ends of the directions, not when some words came to an end.

note: The Tibetan verses of the shade-tree lament are rendered well; the opening line misreads the spreading of the gods' praise.
Faithful translation of the sequence of faith and the teacher's instruction on stabilizing it, with speakers correctly framed.

errors.why: ཤེས་རབ (prajñā) is wisdom/intelligence, not faith; Dharmakīrti says people lack the strength of intellect.

errors.english: The means of valid cognition pramāṇa do not apply to what is absent;
errors.why: The kārikā defines the non-apprehension reason: the non-operation of the means of valid cognition, which has as its result the practice of non-operating toward the non-existent; the English reverses subject and result.

note: Opening of the Pramāṇavārttika: the prose-verse preface wrongly has faith for wisdom, and the dense kārikās on the three kinds of reason are only loosely parsed.

errors.english: Because it impairs the relationship with actual entities.
errors.why: ཉམས here means the relation to real entities is lacking/lost (as the gloss འབྲེལ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར confirms), not that the word impairs a relation.

note: A sound rendering of a technical apoha commentary that follows lemma and gloss closely.

errors.english: If it is certain in that way, how could it arise from something else?
errors.why: The side's opening sentence (because place and time are fixed, smoke, seen where its causes are present and not seen when they are incomplete, has the nature of being produced by them; otherwise it would never occur) is not translated.

fix.find: If it is certain in that way, how could it arise from something else?
fix.replace: [...dependence] is impossible there. Therefore, because place and time are fixed, smoke, which is seen once where [its causes] are present and is not seen when they are incomplete, has the nature of being produced by them; otherwise it would never occur even once. If it is certain in that way, how could it arise from something else?

errors.english: If the head of (Indra) the king of gods
errors.why: བརྒྱ་བྱིན་སྤྱི་བོ renders Skt. śakramūrdhan, 'anthill', the standard example of vapour from an anthill mistaken for smoke, not Indra's head.

fix.find: If the head of (Indra) the king of gods

errors.why: ལྕི་བ here is cow dung (gomaya), the classic example of a lotus-type plant arising from a dissimilar cause, not 'heavy elements'.

note: The argument on the fixed nature of cause and effect is followed, but the side's opening sentence is skipped and two standard Pramāṇa examples (anthill, cow dung) are mistranslated.

errors.english: because that reversal is not established through effort
errors.why: The Tibetan says the reason that is necessarily absent wherever the sādhya is absent is ascertained as excluded effortlessly (without effort); the English inverts this into a lack of effortful establishment.

note: A careful rendering of the discussion of 'certain' in the trairūpya definition and of anvaya/vyatireka, with one muddled final sentence.

errors.english: those individual pillars, which have no individual capacity to support a beam
errors.why: The Tibetan speaks of lifting a beam by those (agents) individually incapable of it; 'pillars' supporting a beam is not in the text and changes the example.

note: Faithful lemma-by-lemma commentary on the whole/parts debate, apart from an invented 'pillars' in the beam example.

errors.english: Indeed, a noble birth prevents one from falling into utter insignificance.
errors.why: The verse argues that birth does not secure worth (men of great lineage are seen to be like dogs); the English asserts the opposite, contradicting its own next sentence.

errors.english: Even if someone lacks natural virtues,
errors.why: The Tibetan says quality does not lie in birth; the idea of gaining worth by associating with the virtuous is not in this verse.

note: The narrative of Candra's youth and the quarrel over names is well rendered; the gnomic verses on birth versus quality are partly misread.
